prompt:
An 86-year-old woman in long-term care with moderate Alzheimer dementia, type 2 diabetes on metformin, and C. difficile infection 8 months ago has been sleepier and eating less for 2 days, and staff say her urine "smells strong." She is afebrile (37.2°C), HR 88, BP 132/70, SpO2 96% on room air, with no dysuria, flank pain, new incontinence, or suprapubic tenderness, and she has no catheter. A nurse sent a urinalysis (moderate leukocyte esterase, nitrite positive, 25 WBC/hpf), and the culture is growing more than 100,000 CFU/mL E. coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin and ciprofloxacin. Creatinine clearance is about 35 mL/min. The facility wants to start antibiotics today. What do you recommend?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Recognize bacteriuria without localizing genitourinary symptoms or systemic signs of infection as asymptomatic bacteriuria that should not be treated.
Withhold antibiotics for the positive urine culture.
Evaluate for alternative causes of lethargy, including dehydration, glucose derangement, medication effects, constipation, urinary retention, pain, and pneumonia.
Check a fingerstick glucose promptly.
Review the medication list for new sedating or anticholinergic drugs.
Obtain a basic metabolic panel and complete blood count to assess for dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and leukocytosis.
Perform a bladder scan for post-void residual volume.
Encourage oral hydration and track intake and output.
Monitor vital signs and mental status every shift for 48 to 72 hours with explicit escalation criteria such as fever, hypotension, rigors, new urinary symptoms, or worsening mental status.
Obtain a chest radiograph if respiratory symptoms, hypoxemia, or abnormal lung findings develop.
Educate staff and family that urine odor or cloudiness alone is not an indication for testing or antibiotics.
Counsel the family that unnecessary antibiotics substantially raise her risk of recurrent C. difficile infection.
Start culture-directed antibiotics promptly if she develops fever, sepsis physiology, or localizing urinary signs.
Support facility stewardship by discouraging urine testing in residents without urinary symptoms or systemic signs.
Recommend cranberry products to prevent future urinary tract infections.
Start topical vaginal estrogen to prevent future urinary tract infections.
Check vitamin B12 and TSH as part of the evaluation for sleepiness.
Check a serum procalcitonin level.
Prescribe nitrofurantoin for 5 to 7 days.
Prescribe ciprofloxacin.
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone.
Give single-dose fosfomycin as a compromise.
Prescribe trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Prescribe amoxicillin-clavulanate.
Start daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent future urinary tract infections.
Start methenamine hippurate for urinary tract infection prevention.
Repeat a urine culture after treatment to document clearance.
Order renal ultrasound or CT imaging to evaluate the bacteriuria.
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to monitor output or obtain specimens.
Attribute the lethargy to a urinary tract infection and stop looking for other causes.
Prescribe quetiapine or another antipsychotic for the altered mental status.
Prescribe phenazopyridine.
Institute routine monthly surveillance urinalyses and cultures.
Transfer her to the emergency department for intravenous antibiotics.
Start prophylactic oral vancomycin alongside an antibiotic for the bacteriuria.
Place her on contact isolation for E. coli bacteriuria.
Refer her to urology for the bacteriuria.
Restrict fluids to reduce incontinence episodes.
